newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK NOT SEEN HIKING KEY RATE IN '97 -ETLA.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK NOT SEEN HIKING KEY RATE IN '97 -ETLA.

text.p: The Bank of Finland is unlikely to raise interest rates before the end of this year although continued firming of the dollar may trigger an uptick in inflation, a domestic economic think-tank said on Wednesday.

"The central bank will probably refrain from touching the tender rate until the outcome of the wage negotiations and state budget proposals are known," the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA) said in a monthly report.
The current pay settlement expires in January 1998 and new wage talks are unlikely to start until late 1997. Parliament's final budget voting usually takes place in mid-December.
"The continued strengthening of the dollar could potentially increase the need for Finland and EU countries to tighten monetary policy to prevent the acceleration of inflation," ETLA said.

The rise of the dollar and sterling -- major invoicing currencies for Finnish industry -- was bolstering the competitiveness of Finnish manufacturers in a situation where demand in Finland's main markets was recovering anyway, it said.
But other factors -- both domestic and international -- were likely to prevent a Finnish key rate hike, it said: primarily, no German tightening was in the cards.

"German inflation is under control and monetary aggregates within the target range. The Bundesbank is not expected to risk missing the EMU criteria by tightening its monetary policy this year," it said.
The markka was under pressure to rise against the German mark due to Finland's wide current account surplus and the consolidation of state finances, ETLA said.
A rate hike could push the markka even stronger.
But in the run-up to EMU, due for start-up in 1999, the Bank of Finland would be keen to keep the markka near the central parity in Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), ETLA said.
"The divergent trends experienced by the Finnish markka are problematic from the standpoint of domestic monetary policy," it said.

The institute supported its conclusion that a unilateral Finnish rate hike was unlikely by stating: "It would be difficult to increase the interest rate differential between Finland and other EU countries so much that it would have any significant effect on domestic demand before entering EMU."
